title: The Roles of Source Citations in Identifying Misinformation and Disinformation: Moderating Effects of Digital Literacy and Information Types
authors: KyungWoo Kim, Seungheon Han, Sung-Bou Kim, Ha Hwang
abstract: This study investigates whether source citations enhance detection of false information and whether their effects depend on digital literacy and information processing style. In an experimental survey of 1,013 South Koreans, citations show no overall effect. However, they significantly improve detection of disinformation—but not misinformation—among individuals with higher digital literacy. Intuitive processing lowers detection ability, and citations do not counteract this tendency. The findings challenge assumptions that transparency universally improves evaluation, showing that citation effectiveness depends on user capabilities and the type of falsehood, and highlighting the need to strengthen digital literacy alongside transparency initiatives.

authors: Emma Turkenburg

title: Ambivalent algorithms, fragile connectedness: How algorithm awareness facets shape responsiveness and insensitivity on TikTok
authors: Dragoș M. Obreja
abstract: This study examines how distinct facets of algorithm awareness are associated with perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR), perceived algorithm insensitivity (PAI), and social connectedness on TikTok. I draw on the algorithm responsiveness process and also treat algorithm awareness as four distinct dimensions (content filtering, automated decision‑making, human–algorithm interplay (HAI), ethical concerns) to examine how each dimension is differentially associated with PAR and PAI and, in turn, with feelings of inclusion and belonging. Using survey data from 305 TikTok users and structural equation modeling, I show that user‑agency‑oriented dimensions, particularly filtering and HAI, are indirectly associated with connectedness via higher responsiveness and lower insensitivity. By contrast, automation operates as an ambivalent structure: it boosts responsiveness yet is negatively associated with connectedness, marking a boundary condition for personalization. Platforms should pair automation disclosures with clearer user recourse, traceable feedback, and human review in high-stakes contexts.

title: News for connection, status and belonging: Exploring the social currency of local news
authors: Jee Young Lee, Sora Park, Janet Fulton
abstract: This paper explores the perception of social currency as a distinct value within local news consumption among audiences. Social currency refers to the value individuals derive from engaging with and sharing news content within their social networks, allowing them to connect, express identity and signal awareness. Drawing on a large-scale mixed-methods study of local news audiences in Australia (survey: n = 7919; interviews and focus groups: n = 84), this study operationalised key dimensions of social currency using factor analysis. The findings confirm that social currency is a separate and measurable construct, distinct from traditional news motivations. It is significantly higher among younger people, men, urban residents and those from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, reflecting how news consumption intersects with social interaction, identity expression and symbolic practices of everyday life.

title: Social Media Savvy? The Use and Effectiveness of Political Parties’ Issue Strategies Across Platforms in the German Federal Election Campaign 2025

title: Apolitical referee or geopolitical actor? How artificial intelligence’s national-origin labels shape credibility in politicized science communication
authors: Junyi Chen, Weixi Zeng, Yi Mou
abstract: Amid the politicization of science and the globalization of technological applications, does the national-origin label of artificial intelligence authors affect their perceived credibility? Drawing on the tension between artificial intelligence as an apolitical referee (machine heuristic) and artificial intelligence as a geopolitical actor like humans (social identity theory and computers-are-social-actors paradigm), two online experiments were conducted in China to examine the role of author type (human, artificial intelligence, and human–artificial intelligence hybrid) and national-origin labels in scientific content with varying degrees of politicization. In a highly politicized context, domestic sources were preferred across all author types, with nationalism amplifying this preference. The effect of artificial intelligence’s national-origin label was significant but weaker than that for human authors. In low-politicized contexts, the national-origin label no longer significantly affected artificial intelligence credibility, while foreign humans were perceived as more credible. These findings highlight the intersecting dynamics of scientific politicization and the public politicized understanding of artificial intelligence technology.

title: The structural contingency model of trust: When variability in perceived trustworthiness of scientists signals critical support
authors: Tenzin Tamang
abstract: Prevailing approaches to measuring public trust in scientists rely on facet averages that overlook within-person variability, a dimension traditional views equate with ambivalence or attitudinal weakness. This study introduces the Structural Contingency Model of Trust (SCMT), proposing that the functional meaning of this variability is contingent on an individual’s overall trust level. In a Bayesian analysis of survey data from 68 countries ( N = 69,534), higher Trust Level (mean across 12 facets) strongly predicted greater general confidence in scientists. Critically, a credible interaction effect supported the SCMT: among highly trusting individuals, greater Trust Variability (variance across facets) was associated with the highest probability of reporting a great deal of confidence in scientists. This Critical Support profile suggests that variability can signify robust, differentiated engagement rather than evaluative weakness, offering a nuanced framework for understanding the complex, multidimensional nature of public trust in scientists.

title: Antecedents of Disclosure: What Transparency Measures Social Media Users in the United States Want From Paid Political Influencers
authors: Martin J. Riedl, Benjamin D. Horne, Matthew J. A. Craig, Michael R. Kotowski, Catherine A. Luther
abstract: At the heels of the 2024 U.S. presidential election, public attention turned to the role social media influencers played in Donald J. Trump’s decisive win. In the United States, unlike influencers promoting commercial brands, political influencers – that is, social media influencers who associate themselves with political causes – are not required to disclose whether they got paid in exchange for promoting a political organization, party, or campaign. Through a survey of U.S. social media users ( n = 906), this study explores people’s attitudes toward paid political influencer disclosure. We find that political partisanship impacts support for disclosure: being more conservative is connected to lessened support for disclosure, yet disclosure is of strong bipartisan concern regardless. Our study documents that social media users who care for authenticity – a core currency in influencer ecosystems running on parasocial relationships – also exhibit higher support for disclosure. Yet, at the same time, caveating this empirical relationship between authenticity and disclosure, we also found that those who consumed more political influencer content exhibited lower support for disclosure, pinpointing the normalization of a digital ecology replete with sponsored content. Our study has implications for the broader political communication ecology: As transparency for paid political influencer activities emerges as a topic of public concern, platforms and regulators should advance efforts that provide disclosure about paid political influencer activities to social media users.

title: Sharing the Alternative – The Role of Digital Platforms for Alternative News-Sharing Behavior
authors: Felix Gaisbauer, Jakob Ohme
abstract: In a time of growing concerns over factual accuracy in the public sphere, alternative news media have emerged as a counterpoint to traditional mass media. In Germany, many online-only outlets cater to a rising audience, driven by distinct goals, standards, and funding structures compared to what they term ‘elite media’. Digital platforms are vital to their success, enabling audience growth with minimal financial investment and bypassing legacy media systems’ critique and verification mechanisms. Their reach, however, relies on followers sharing content and leveraging social media’s network effect to amplify niche information. Yet, the sharing habits of alternative news audiences remain understudied. This study uses original survey data from over 2,000 German alternative news users (collected in September 2023), exploring whether these patterns drive alternative media’s rise as a counterweight to established journalism. We investigate users’ sharing activity, their motivations for sharing news or refraining from it, and sociodemographic/ideological predictors for alternative news sharing.

title: “Fairness Labels” in Feeds: Process Disclosures, Provenance, and User Choice Among Short‑Video Creators in Mainland China
authors: Dandan Liu, Guangrui Fan
abstract: Algorithmically ranked feeds allocate attention in ways that can reproduce inequalities in visibility. We test whether a compact, feed-level process disclosure —a banner describing exposure-safeguard governance, paired with provenance cues and in-situ user-choice affordances—improves perceived procedural justice, distributive fairness, and legitimacy among short-video creators in mainland China. In a mobile-first online experiment with 1,154 research-verified PRC creators in the People’s Republic of China (PRC), participants viewed a realistic feed randomized to No label , Personalization notice , or Fairness disclosure ; within the fairness condition, we factorially varied frame (Safeguards/Parity/Quotas/Exposure-fairness), issuer provenance (platform vs. independent audit), and disclosure depth (minimal badge vs. brief rationale). The compound fairness disclosure increased perceived procedural justice, distributive fairness, and legitimacy relative to both controls and was accompanied by lower self-censorship and higher voice intentions. Effects were directionally stronger in civic/news contexts and among creators who self-identified as marginalized or previously down-ranked. Within-arm exploratory diagnostics suggested that quota-like parity framing may yield directionally lower legitimacy than exposure-fairness framing, while audit cues produced directionally positive but imprecise trust gains. Backfire checks found no implied-unfairness spillover for unlabeled items and no interaction with per-item AI-content labels, although AI labels reduced perceived accuracy. Together, these findings suggest that governance-aligned micro-disclosures can function as procedural visibility signals for creators, while underscoring the importance of verifiable claims and careful disclosure design.

title: Incivility Among Politicians: Driven by Rational Minds or Personal Drives?
authors: Željko Poljak, Bart Maes
abstract: There is growing concern about politicians engaging in incivility by mocking and insulting each other. While prior research often explains such discourse through rational choice, emerging work highlights the role of politicians’ individual traits, such as their personality. Yet, a unified theoretical account of how rationality and individual predispositions interact to shape harmful elite discourse is lacking. Drawing on foundational insights from psychology, we argue that politicians’ discourse reflects primarily rational considerations, which are moderated by their individual predispositions, leading to uncivil communication between politicians. We test this notion using elite survey data, unobtrusive measures of their individual traits, and direct observations of politicians’ social media communication in Belgium – a rare integration of psychological and behavioral evidence at the elite level. The results show that politicians’ use of uncivil discourse responds to rational considerations, but that the strength of this response depends on their individual predispositions. These findings demonstrate that individual traits moderate how politicians translate rational incentives into harmful discourse, providing a more nuanced account of the causes of elite incivility.

title: An Effort Made for Whom? Exploring Ministers’ Public Approval and Name Recognition in Relation to Their Media Activity
authors: Mads Fuglsang Hove, Jonas Krogh Madsen, Peter Heyn Nielsen
abstract: In many democracies, cabinet ministers find themselves in a difficult situation, juggling a demanding administrative job with political responsibilities and the need to communicate and campaign to secure reelection. With the rise of social media, this balance is becoming increasingly unstable. However, the tangible benefits of media visibility outside election campaigns remain unclear, making it difficult to determine whether such efforts yield meaningful political returns. This study examines and compares whether Danish ministers’ media activities—both in traditional and social media—impact their name recognition and popularity in the Danish population. We utilize thirty-two nationally representative opinion polls conducted between March 2020 and May 2024 and merge these with extensive records of all Danish ministers’ Facebook activity and appearances in traditional media outlets throughout the same period. Overall, our findings show that ministers’ activity in traditional media is associated with only minor gains in name recognition, while social media activity has either zero or minimal gains in popularity. Moreover, breaking down these correlations across different types of Facebook interactions and traditional media outlets suggests a trade-off between reaching and being perceived favorably by voters, showing the multifaceted nature of (social) media activity. Consequently, while we do not rule out any significant effects of social media on voters’ perceptions, we argue that social media activity is no panacea for politicians to improve their public popularity and name recognition.

title: Populism, radicalism, and protest mobilization by parties in Europe
authors: Leonhard Schmidt, Bruno Castanho Silva
abstract: As European democracies struggle with a ‘crisis of representation’, populist parties appear to be instrumental in channeling popular discontent with governments across the continent, including through protests. While contemporary theories propose a strong connection between populism and protest mobilization, this has seldom been tested in a comparative perspective. At the same time, research has found that radical parties are more likely to mobilize for protests, and those parties are often also populist. We empirically disentangle these relationships with a comprehensive dataset of 4.8 million Facebook posts by all active sitting MPs in all EU27 national parliaments plus the UK between 2018 and 2023, using large language models to identify protest-related posts and those that announce protest events. Findings show that it is particularly radical parties mobilizing their followers, with populism itself having little additional explanatory power. This is the first cross-national, longitudinal evaluation of a much-touted theoretical connection between populist parties and protest mobilization, finding that it appears smaller and more conditional than prior research proposed.

title: Cool Citizens? How Affectively Unpolarized Citizens View and Participate in Democracy
authors: Peter Luca Versteegen, Joseph B. Phillips, Lilliana Mason
abstract: Does affective polarization change how citizens view and participate in democracy? We posit that the answer to this crucial question depends on how affectively un polarized citizens view and participate in democracy. Yet, the most common operationalization of affective polarization––measuring sympathy ratings for one party relative to another––does not differentiate between people’s absolute sympathy ratings for the parties, which may mask essential heterogeneity among unpolarized citizens. This paper theorizes the methodological origin of this heterogeneity, describes it, and highlights its implications. Cluster analyses and regressions from three nationally representative surveys in the US provide three conclusions. First, substantial shares of the US population are affectively un polarized. Second, unpolarized citizens cluster into two groups: one feeling lukewarm and one feeling cold toward both parties. Third, these unpolarized groups report diverging democratic attitudes and participation patterns. We discuss the methodological implications and the need for future research on affectively unpolarized citizens.

title: The Role of Attention and Norm Perception in Online Comments’ Impact on Attitudes toward Sunscreen: An Eye-Tracking Approach

title: The WHO Said What? Interaction of Source Credibility and Readers’ Prior Beliefs in the Reading of Social-Media Posts
authors: Oskari J. Virtanen, Johanna K. Kaakinen
abstract: Evaluating sources is an essential skill in our misinformation-riddled media environment. However, previous studies suggest that people tend not to engage with source information during reading, and very little research exists on how source credibility and readers’ beliefs interact on social media. We examined how source credibility and prior beliefs affect reading social-media posts. Finnish university students ( N = 83) first filled out a questionnaire measuring beliefs on eight controversial topics and then read 76 mock-up tweets on these topics while their eye movements were recorded. The sources of the tweets were pretested to be either credible or noncredible sources for the topic. Eye-movement results indicate that when credible sources say something belief-inconsistent, or if noncredible sources something belief-consistent, reading of the tweet is slower, and more attention is paid to the sources. Findings suggest that these “source-belief” inconsistencies disrupt reading and elicit deeper processing of source information.

title: The shrinking landscape of linguistic diversity in the age of large language models
authors: Zhivar Sourati, Farzan Karimi-Malekabadi, Meltem Ozcan, Colin McDaniel, Alireza Ziabari, Jackson Trager, Ala N. Tak, Meng Chen, Fred Morstatter, Morteza Dehghani
abstract: Language is far more than a communication tool; it encodes a wealth of information about a person’s identity, psychological state and social context, providing valuable insights for diverse fields including psychology, marketing and healthcare. Across three studies spanning seven datasets in different domains and over 880,000 texts, we show that the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) as writing assistants is linked to declines in linguistic diversity, interfering with the societal and psychological insights language provides. While core content is retained when LLMs polish and rewrite texts, LLMs also homogenize writing styles, reducing writing-complexity variance by a statistically significant 21–50% across datasets and models (P ≤ 0.05), and amplify patterns associated with dominant characteristics while suppressing others, emphasizing conformity over individuality. These trends hold across different LLMs, prompts and contexts, with potential implications for diagnostic processes, personalization efforts, hiring assessments and cultural preservation.

title: Quantifying the prevalence and impact of overreaching causal claims in social science
authors: Calvin Isch, Timothy Dörr, Neil Fasching, Grace Jennings, Duncan J. Watts
abstract: Across the social sciences, many studies use cross-sectional designs that reveal associations but are generally unable to support direct causal claims, yet authors of such articles may make or imply causal claims anyway. Here, to examine the prevalence of such ‘overreaching’ causal language, we analysed 194,631 cross-sectional articles using large language models. Over the period 1980–2024, an average of 46% of articles contained causal language in their titles or abstracts, where the annual rate has risen almost threefold since 2000 from 20% to 60%. To examine the effects of such language, we conducted a human-subjects experiment ( N = 1, 105), finding that readers frequently indicate abstracts with this phrasing provide causal evidence but that methodological labels ( β = −0.4, 95% confidence interval −0.56 to −0.19) and associational wording ( β = −0.3, 95% confidence interval −0.43 to −0.07) reduce this tendency. Experiments with five LLMs revealed that model summaries of these articles ( N = 100 each) can amplify causal overstatement, removing hedges and introducing causal claims where articles used strictly associational phrasing; however, prompting caution diminishes this pattern.

title: Social technology use and life satisfaction in a five-wave panel study of US adults
authors: Kostadin Kushlev, Kibum Moon, Matt Motyl, Nathanael J. Fast, Juliana Schroeder
abstract: Here, in five waves of panel data (N = 1,966 US adults), we examined associations between life satisfaction and self-reported use of ten common social technologies measured every 3 months on a six-point frequency scale from ‘I did not use’ to ‘multiple times daily’. At this measurement level and timescale, Bayesian and frequentist random-intercept cross-lagged panel models showed little credible evidence that any social technology use predicts subsequent life satisfaction. In the reverse direction, increases in life satisfaction predicted only modest increases in (video) calling in select demographic groups. In analyses comparing different people, frequency of texting was associated with higher life satisfaction, whereas frequency of YouTube and TikTok use was associated with lower life satisfaction. Despite limited ability to detect within-person change due to temporal stability in responses, the absence of cross-lagged effects is informative: there is scant evidence of a meaningful relationship between social technology use and subsequent life satisfaction.

title: Personality pairing improves human–AI collaboration
authors: Harang Ju, Sinan Aral
journal_full: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
abstract: Here we examine how AI agent “personalities” interact with human personalities to shape human–AI collaboration and performance. In a large-scale, preregistered randomized experiment, we paired 1,258 participants with AI agents prompted to exhibit varying levels of the Big Five personality traits. These human–AI teams produced 7,266 display ads for a real think tank, which we evaluated using 1,168 independent human raters, and a field experiment on X that generated nearly 5 million impressions. We found that human and AI personalities individually shaped ad quality and teamwork and that human–AI personality pairings directly influenced ad quality. For example, extraverted humans paired with conscientious AI produced the lowest quality ads, followed by conscientious humans paired with agreeable AI and neurotic humans paired with conscientious AI. In the field experiment, ad quality significantly influenced ad performance, measured by click-through rates and cost-per-click. Together, these results demonstrate that personality pairing can improve human–AI collaboration and performance. They also motivate future research on the complex implications of AI personalization for human–AI collaboration, teamwork, and performance.
